Jim Crow Laws. State and local statutes enacted primarily in the American South from the eighteen seventies through the nineteen sixties that enforced racial segregation and discriminated against African Americans, named after a racist minstrel show character. These laws mandated the separation of Black and white people in schools, public facilities, transportation, housing, and every other area of life under the doctrine of separate but equal, upheld in Plessy v. Ferguson in eighteen ninety-six. Jim Crow laws were enforced both through legal punishment and extrajudicial violence, systematizing white supremacy and disenfranchising Black voters through literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses.

They proliferated after Reconstruction ended in eighteen seventy-seven, reversing the gains African Americans had made. Rather than using explicit racial language, which the Fourteenth Amendment prohibited, these laws enforced segregation through facially neutral statutes that applied only where race was involved, such as no intermarriage. They governed schools, transportation, hotels, restaurants, parks, water fountains, cemeteries, and even blood banks.

Literacy tests required voters to read and explain complex passages, administered with racist discretion. Poll taxes levied a tax on voting but included grandfather clause exemptions for voters whose grandfather had voted, allowing poor white men to vote while excluding formerly enslaved Black men. White primaries excluded Black voters from Democratic primary elections, effectively excluding them from the only competitive elections in the one-party South.

In practice, facilities provided to Black people were vastly inferior to those for white people, contradicting the supposedly equal part of separate but equal. Plessy remained the law for fifty-eight years until overturned in Brown v. Board of Education in nineteen fifty-four. Legal penalties for violating segregation statutes included fines and imprisonment, but the enforcement mechanism extended beyond the courts. The Ku Klux Klan and white mobs used extrajudicial violence, and economic coercion through loss of employment, housing, and credit targeted Black people who challenged segregation.

Jim Crow laws created a rigid caste system denying African Americans equal access to education, economic opportunity, political power, and basic dignity. They were the legal foundation for wealth inequality between Black and white Americans that persists today. The Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four prohibited discrimination in public accommodations, while the Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five prohibited voter suppression mechanisms. Jim Crow laws connect to the Reconstruction era, the period they reversed, to segregation itself, to African American history and the lived experience of Jim Crow subordination, to the Civil Rights Movement that challenged and dismantled them, to the Fourteenth Amendment, to Brown v. Board of Education which began dismantling Jim Crow in schools, to the Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five which banned Jim Crow voting suppression, to the Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four which banned Jim Crow discrimination in public accommodations, and to systemic racism, of which Jim Crow laws were a foundational mechanism.
